lecture19.title: Neuron, Neural Networks, LLMs and Agents

sections.title: Neuron, neural networks, LLMs and agents
From a neuron to agents that communicate

teaching.text: **A neuron takes a vector and returns one number.** Each input is multiplied by its weight, and the products are added to give the output. This weighted sum is an **inner product**. A neural network joins many such operations into layers, so one input vector becomes a **decision vector**, with a response for each possible answer.
children: **A large language model takes many vectors and predicts what comes next.** Fifteen token vectors pass through five layers in the example. Each layer changes their representations through its weights, and the final output is the sixteenth vector, a **probability distribution** over the next token. The values express which continuations the model treats as more or less likely.

teaching.text: **An agentic system connects several LLMs into a graph.** The Outline model develops a plan, the Write model produces a draft, the Critic model evaluates it, the Revise model changes it, and the Final model produces the answer. The connection between Critic and Revise forms a loop, allowing a revision to be evaluated again.
children: The agents communicate through **language**. One model’s written output becomes information another model can use, so the graph coordinates whole language models rather than individual neurons. The agents can speak to each other in English, while the models can also work in other human languages and computer languages.

teaching.text: **Inference uses inner products, and learning uses SGD with dynamic programming.** Inference processes the current inputs with the learned weights. **Stochastic gradient descent**, or SGD, changes weights to reduce prediction error, while backpropagation uses **dynamic programming** to organize the backward calculation. These operations support the small network as well as the language models joined into the agentic graph.

**Predicting the next word is difficult because the prediction depends on information spread through the sequence.** A language model therefore uses many layers of processing. Each layer receives representations of the input and changes them before passing them onward, giving the following layer more useful information for the prediction.
children: **Within a layer, several heads work in parallel.** A head is one of the processing components that contributes to the layer’s representation. The heads are described as different experts because each can contribute a different part of the information the layer uses. They work alongside one another rather than waiting for one head to finish before another begins.

teaching.text: **The layer brings the heads’ contributions together.** The result is an improved set of representations, written as **x**, for the sequence. A representation is the information carried by a vector about an input item. Combining several contributions lets that representation incorporate more than one head contributes on its own.
children: **The next layer repeats the process with the representations it receives.** It has parallel heads whose contributions are combined again. The model therefore develops its representations through a succession of layers, rather than making its final prediction directly from the original input vectors.

teaching.text: **Heads and layers add different kinds of structure.** Heads provide parallel contributions within one processing stage, while layers provide successive stages that refine the vectors further. The prediction at the end depends on these contributions being combined within stages and developed across stages.

sections.title: A dynamical rule across time and depth

teaching.text: **A dynamical system takes a state, applies a rule, and uses the resulting state as input again.** In the oscillator example, the state contains position **x** and velocity **v**. It begins with position one and velocity zero, and repeatedly updating those two quantities produces the changing motion.
children: **Position and velocity take turns being updated.** The new position uses the old velocity, and the new velocity then uses that new position. The step size **h** determines how far the calculation advances at each update. Position traces a cosine-like oscillation while velocity follows a shifted oscillation, so a simple repeated rule builds an entire changing trajectory.

teaching.text: **Jordan’s recurrent network also feeds its output back into its input.** Plan units and state units feed a hidden layer, which produces an output. That output is copied into the state units, and their small self-loops preserve a fading trace of earlier states. The weights are reused at each time step, allowing recent outputs to influence the next output in a sequence of speech movements.
children: **In the LLM comparison, depth plays the role of time.** Fifteen vectors enter the first layer and are transformed by its weights. The resulting vectors enter the next layer, where another transformation takes place. Following one number upward through the layers gives a sequence of changing values, which can be drawn as a curve even though it is not the oscillator’s cosine.

teaching.text: **The rules are organized differently in these systems.** The oscillator and Jordan network apply the same rule repeatedly as time advances. The LLM uses a separate set of weights at each layer, so its successive transformations follow the depth of the network. What connects the examples is the dependence of each new state on the state produced just before it.
The small stock-return graph traces Small, Medium and Large series over the same period. They fluctuate, rise and fall over the years, giving another example of quantities changing over time.

sections.title: One prediction task for different sequences

teaching.text: The page starts with **15 vectors**, **x₁ to x₁₅**, an empty **x₁₆**, and the question **vectors of what?**
children: An LLM reads a sequence of vectors and predicts the next one.

teaching.text: **A sentence cut into 15 words**.
children: “The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the ___.”
**x₁₆ is the missing word**, and getting it right uses words from far back in the sentence.

teaching.text: **A spectrogram cut into 15 frames** and **an image cut into 16 patches**.
children: The spectrogram spans 0 to 5 kHz over time, and **x₁₆ is the next frame**.
The image of a house, tree and sun is read row by row, and **x₁₆ is the missing bottom-right patch**.

teaching.text: **A protein, the insulin B chain**, read as **15 amino acids**.
children: F V N Q H L C G S H L V E A L fold into a helix.
**x₁₆ is the next residue, Y**.

teaching.text: **The LLM only ever sees vectors.**
children: Words, sounds, pixels and molecules become the same kind of input.
**One machine asks one question, what is x₁₆?**

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?

teaching.text: **Which sequences can be English words?** Three rows build the answer.
children: Twenty **one-syllable words** like Don, mat, sit, cup and fish each have one consonant, one vowel and one consonant.
**A simple syllable in English can have a consonant, then a vowel, then a consonant.**

teaching.text: **Clusters** come before the vowel as **onsets** and after it as **codas**.
children: Onsets appear in split, flat, black, glad and stop.
Codas appear in desk, box, help, milk and lamp.
Each has a starred impossible twin, *sblit, *lfat, *bnack, *dlad, *tsop, *desb, *bokp, *hepl, *mikl, *lapm.

teaching.text: Order decides which clusters are allowed.
children: flat and *lfat, help and *hepl, lamp and *lapm use the same letters in different orders.
The allowed order mirrors around the vowel.
**Only certain sequences are allowed before the vowel and after the vowel.**

teaching.text: Long words are built from several syllables.
children: ba·na·na, win·dow, pump·kin, nap·kin, At·lan·tic, ath·lete, ad·mit and spa·ghet·ti all break into syllables.
t·l, th·l and d·m sit across breaks, so *tlantic, *thlete and *dmit fail as word starts.
ng ends a syllable, as in ring, so *ngapkin fails.

teaching.text: **A long word is a chain of syllables**, each following the same rules.
children: **t·l is fine across a break, but tl cannot start a syllable.**
This sound-sequence knowledge is **phonotactics**, and speakers know it without instruction.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge

teaching.text: The quiz reveals **phonotactic knowledge through GPT learning**.
children: Each item starts an English word, and the task is to **guess the next letter**.
The starts are ra_, sp_, k_, skr_, m_, bram_, b_, f_ and sh_.

teaching.text: After a vowel, many letters fit.
children: **ra_** takes t, n, r, l and more, since **after a vowel almost anything** can follow.

teaching.text: Word starts allow only a few letters.
children: **sp_**, **b_** and **f_** take **l, r or a vowel**, never *spn, *bn or *fn.
**k_** takes a vowel or **n**, as in knee, never *kt.
**sh_** takes a vowel or **r**, as in shrimp, never *shb.

teaching.text: Some starts leave one kind of answer.
children: **skr_** and **m_** take only a vowel, never *skrl or *mb.
**bram_** nearly forces b, as in bramble, unless a new syllable starts.

teaching.text: **Guessing the next letter is predicting x₁₆.**
children: A **GPT trained only on this game learns English sounds and spelling**.
Its distribution is broad after ra_ and sharply peaked after skr_.

sections.title: Design an agentic system for English syllables

teaching.text: **An LLM learns by guessing a hidden word and then adjusting its weights.** In the sentence “The chef cracks the,” the last word is hidden. The model reads the earlier words and has to predict the word that comes next.
children: **Each earlier word gives a clue about the hidden word.** “The,” “chef,” “cracks” and “the” are each linked to the empty slot. These links are **interdependencies**, which are relationships in which one part of a sequence helps predict another part. A chef who cracks something makes a food word likely.

teaching.text: **The model does not know the answer, so it spreads its bets.** A bet is the probability the model gives to one possible word. The largest bet is on “egg,” a smaller bet is on “nut,” and the smallest is on “code.” All three could follow, but the earlier words make “egg” the most likely.

**Learning is nudging the weights so that these guesses get better.** A nudge is a small change to a weight. After the true word is revealed, the weights change a little, so the right word gets a bigger bet the next time.
children: **The same idea holds when the signal contains more than words.** The signal is the sequence the model reads. It can hold **words, sounds and images** together, and the model still guesses a hidden piece from the other pieces. The content of the signal changes, while the way the model learns stays the same.

sections.title: Text, speech and images in three different forms

teaching.text: **An LLM can only read a row of vectors, and not all information arrives in that form.** Text, speech and images reach the model in three different forms. Speech and images have to be converted before the model can use them.
children: **Text is already a row of pieces.** The sentence “Now crack the egg” separates into the pieces “Now,” “crack,” “the” and “egg.” Each piece can become one vector, so text is easy to give to the model.

teaching.text: **Speech is air pressure changing in time.** The pressure goes up and down continuously, and nothing in the sound marks where one word stops and the next one starts. There are no words in the sound itself.
**An image is a grid of light.** Each position in the grid has its own brightness and colour. The image of an egg in a pan contains no words either, and its pieces are not arranged in a row.
children: **The first job is a conversion.** All three forms have to become rows of vectors, because a row of vectors is all the LLM can read. Once speech and images are rows too, one model can read them together with text.

sections.title: Speech becomes a row of frame vectors

teaching.text: **Speech is converted by slicing time into short frames.** A **frame** is one short slice of the sound. The speech is cut at regular points in time, and each slice is about 20 milliseconds long.
children: **The slices go through a speech encoder.** A **speech encoder** is a neural network that was trained on a large amount of audio. It receives the slices of sound and turns each one into a vector.

teaching.text: **One vector comes out for each slice.** Different slices contain different sounds, so their vectors hold different numbers. The different shades in the columns under the encoder stand for those different numbers.

**One second of speech becomes 50 vectors.** Each slice lasts about 20 milliseconds, and 50 slices of that length fill one second. The vectors stay in time order, so the earliest slice comes first in the row.
children: **Speech is now a row, just like a sentence.** A sentence is a row of word vectors, and the sliced speech is a row of frame vectors. The LLM reads both the same way, one vector after another.

sections.title: Images become a row of patch vectors

teaching.text: **An image is converted by cutting it into patches.** A **patch** is one small square of the image. The image of an egg in a pan is cut by a grid into 16 patches, 4 across and 4 down.
children: **The patches are laid out in a row, in reading order.** Reading order means left to right along the top, then left to right along the next line down, the way a page is read. The image is now a sequence with a fixed order, like a sentence.

teaching.text: **The patches go through a vision encoder.** A **vision encoder** turns each patch into a vector, in the same way the speech encoder turns each slice of sound into a vector.
**One vector comes out for each patch.** The 16 patches give 16 vectors, and the vectors keep the order of the patches. The image has become a row that the LLM can read.
children: **Real systems use much smaller patches.** The 4 by 4 grid keeps the example simple. Real systems use patches of 14 to 16 pixels, so one image gives hundreds of vectors.

teaching.text: **Image patches, speech frames and words are placed in one row.** The image patches come first, the speech frames come next, and the words come last. The words are “Now,” “crack” and “the,” and the last word is hidden.
children: **The earlier words still give clues.** “Now,” “crack” and “the” each help the model guess the hidden word. These are the same dependencies between words that a model uses when its row holds only text.

teaching.text: **Clues now also come from the other senses.** A patch that contains an egg helps predict the hidden word, and so does the sound of cracking. A link between two different kinds of signal is a **cross-modal dependency**.
**The game is exactly the same as before.** The model guesses the hidden piece from the pieces it can read. It then learns from how good the guess was.
children: **The source of the clues is what changes.** With text alone, every clue is a word. In the combined row, a clue can also be an image patch or a speech frame, so the model has more information for the same guess.

sections.title: Three cute puppies as an image, speech and words

teaching.text: **One event can be given to the model in three forms.** The example is “three cute puppies.” It appears as an image of three puppies, as the phrase spoken aloud, and as the three written words.
children: **The image is cut into 18 patches.** The grid has 3 rows of 6 patches. As with the egg, each patch is one piece of the image.

teaching.text: **The spoken phrase is a spectrogram.** A **spectrogram** displays sound with time running from left to right. A higher position means a higher frequency, and a darker area means more energy.

**Each word occupies its own stretch of time.** “Three” comes first, “cute” comes second and “puppies” comes last. Each thin column of the spectrogram is one frame. The speech was made with a speech synthesizer, an MBROLA diphone voice.
children: **The image, the sound and the words are three views of one event.** In training, all three go into one row. The model then plays the same game on that row, in which one piece is hidden and the model guesses it.

sections.title: Training example 1 predicts the next word

teaching.text: **In the first training example, the hidden piece is a word.** The row holds the image first, then the sound, then the words. The words are “three” and “cute,” and the last word is hidden.
children: **With the words alone, many endings fit.** “Kittens,” “puppies” and “babies” can all follow “three cute.” The model’s bets are spread out across the three words, and no word is far ahead.

teaching.text: **The image and the sound add clues.** The image contains puppies, and the sound contains the spoken word “puppies.” With these clues the bet piles up on “puppies,” and “kittens” and “babies” get very small bets.
**The true word is then revealed, and the model is graded.** The grade depends on how much the model bet on the true word. The true word is “puppies,” and the model bet 0.85 on it.
children: **A large bet on the truth gives a small nudge.** The model bet a lot on the true word, so the error is small. Because the error is small, the weights move only a little.

sections.title: Training example 2 predicts a sound frame

teaching.text: **In the second training example, the hidden piece is a frame of sound.** The row is reordered so the image comes first, then the words, then the sound. This is like teaching the model to speak a sentence it was given. The sound is predicted frame by frame from left to right, and the frames to the right have not been heard yet.
children: **The first clue comes from the earlier frames.** The speaker’s voice and the **formants** (frequency regions with strong energy) change smoothly. Because they change smoothly, the last few frames say a lot about the next frame.

teaching.text: **The words say which sound should come next.** Here the next sound is the vowel in “pup.” The image contains puppies, so it backs up the words. The image is a weaker clue in this example.

**A frame is a column of numbers.** Each number is how much energy there is in one frequency band, and 16 bands are displayed. The model’s guess is close to the true frame but not exact. The error is how far apart each number in the guess is from the matching number in the truth.
children: **That error nudges the weights.** The weights change so that the next guess for a frame is closer. Some systems predict a code for each frame instead of the raw numbers.

sections.title: Training example 3 predicts an image patch

teaching.text: **In the third training example, the hidden piece is a patch of the image.** The row is reordered again so the words come first, then the sound, then the image. This is like teaching the model to draw what it was told. The patches are predicted in reading order, and the patches that are not drawn yet are faded.
children: **The earlier patches give the first clue.** Above the hidden patch is background. To its left are two puppies, so the model has already seen what a puppy in this image looks like.

teaching.text: **The words help in a different way.** “Three” says a third puppy must appear, and only two have been drawn. “Puppies” says to expect dog ears. The sound carries the same words, so it is a backup for the text.

**The guess is a blurry puppy ear in the average colour of the first two puppies.** The true patch belongs to a dark puppy. The biggest error is therefore the colour, because nothing in the words, the sound or the earlier patches said the third puppy would be dark.
children: **That error nudges the weights.** Only systems that also produce images are trained this way. Systems that only read images usually skip this step.

sections.title: Every piece can be the hidden one

teaching.text: **Any piece of the row can be the hidden one.** The hidden piece can be a word, a sound frame or an image patch. In each case, the words, the sound and the image each give a clue.
children: **For a hidden word, all three senses point to “puppies.”** The words “three cute” call for a plural noun. The sound helps because the word was just spoken. The image helps because it contains puppies.

teaching.text: **For a hidden frame, the sound itself says the most about what comes next.** The voice and the formants carry on from the earlier frames. The words say which sound comes next, and the image backs up which word is being said.

**For a hidden patch, the image itself says how the patch should continue.** The fur and the background carry on from the earlier patches. The word “three” says one more puppy is coming, and the sound gives the same words in heard form.
children: **Clues from the same sense and clues from other senses do different jobs.** A clue from the same sense mostly says how the signal continues, as with grammar, smooth formants, and fur and background. Clues from the other senses mostly say what the thing is, which here is puppies, three of them. Training on all three senses together helps because each sense fills gaps the others leave.

sections.title: Talking back, and what is new

teaching.text: **For the model to speak, sound is compressed into discrete codes.** A code is a number that stands for a short piece of sound, such as 417, 82 or 903. Each code works like a new word added to the model’s vocabulary.
children: **The model predicts the next code exactly as it predicts the next word.** The earlier codes give clues about the hidden code, so producing speech is the same guessing game again.

teaching.text: **A decoder turns the codes back into sound.** The **decoder** takes the row of predicted codes and produces a sound wave that can be heard.

**Three things are new.** The first is a shared currency, in which everything becomes vectors in one row. The second is data where the senses appear together. The third is a schedule that protects what was already learned.
children: **The learning rule stays the same.** The model still finds the dependencies in the signal. The signal has become wider, because it now holds words, sounds and images.
